mentions.text: Web services don’t cache private info across users. Consider a file storage service. You might have the client hash the file before uploading and skip the upload if you already have a file with that hash. This is smart design if it’s being used as a sync service. You might make this happen systemwide, so if user A uploads a file and then B uploads the same file, B can skip the upload. This must not be done. Your service now becomes an oracle that tells you whether someone else using the service has uploaded a particular document. Find a document that gets filled out with name and date of birth, and if you know the name of someone using the service and they’ve uploaded a filled-out copy of this document, you can discover their date of birth. Put more concretely, it’s OK if Netflix caches across users (technically, someone can leak the data that someone in the metro area has recently watched Morbius, but the amount of data leaked is too small to matter) but not ok if Gmail does it. A KV cache shared across users is pretty dangerous and I’m surprised anyone does this, aside from some known fixed prefixes.

mentions.text: Because of nonlinearities in the exponents. Each win compounds faster than compounding of a loss. A near inverse of the Kelly criterion. In mature markets (financial services in 2008) the risk is a zero sum game and there is no super-exponential compounding. In fact the opposite holds true - if you have more AUM your ability to extract proportionally more money from the market diminishes. In the startup world, where you create new markets, Jevons paradox grants you that super-exponential growth. Nvidia, SpaceX and probably a few others.. are the rare ones that are huge, and yet non-saturated market creators. Apple is saturated. So is Meta, Netflix, Alphabet, etc. Microsoft is a wildcard a bit with OpenAI stake, but.. maybe? Amazon is habitually saturated but actually most adapted to it.
